sources.cite: Kiernan TJ, Ajani AE, Yan BP. Management of access site and systemic complications of percutaneous coronary and peripheral interventions. J Invasive Cardiol 2008;20:463-469
sources.note: Relayed from the PCCN case femoral-access-retroperitoneal-bleed, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14 through a summarizing fetch. Hypotension after an endovascular procedure should always include retroperitoneal bleeding in the differential; lower abdominal or flank pain and an acute hematocrit drop suggest it; a high puncture above the inguinal ligament is the main risk; confirmed by CT of the abdomen and pelvis; stable patients: transfusion, heparin reversal with protamine and close blood pressure monitoring; unstable patients: volume resuscitation and urgent angiography from the other side, with balloon, covered stent or surgery. A 2008 review: no newer society guideline on this complication was found.

sources.cite: Sui YG, Teng SY, Qian J, et al. Cross-sectional study of retroperitoneal hematoma after invasive intervention in a Chinese population. Exp Ther Med 2020;20(4):2975-2984
sources.note: Relayed from the PCCN case femoral-access-retroperitoneal-bleed, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14 through a summarizing fetch. Incidence 0.15-6% in published series; 'the most serious and potentially fatal complication of percutaneous intervention'; early signs are indistinct until hypovolemia; pain (abdominal, leg, waist) was the most common symptom; most cases were managed conservatively with transfusion; embolization or emergency surgery for the rest.

sources.cite: Kern MJ. Back to basics: femoral artery access and hemostasis. Cath Lab Digest 2013;21(10)
sources.note: Relayed from the PCCN case femoral-access-retroperitoneal-bleed, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-14 through a summarizing fetch. The needle enters the artery higher than the skin entry site, so manual compression goes over the artery about an inch cranial to the skin incision; firm pressure for 15-20 minutes, longer on antiplatelet drugs; pedal pulses checked every 2-3 minutes during compression; more than 500 mL can be lost before anyone notices.

The restrictive thresholds (hemoglobin 7 g/dL; 8 with preexisting cardiovascular disease) are for hemodynamically stable hospitalized adults; they do not apply to active hemorrhage.

sources.note: Relayed from the PCCN case femoral-access-retroperitoneal-bleed, not re-read for this band; its note: Read 2026-11-16 in the publisher's PDF (open access, from Universidad Europea's repository; summarizing fetch with quotes). Recommendation 9 (Grade 1B): 'We recommend the use of repeated Hb and/or Hct measurements as a laboratory marker for bleeding, as an initial value in the normal range may mask early-phase bleeding.' Used only for one teaching point: a single normal hemoglobin does not rule out early bleeding, so it is repeated.
